title: Japa: the Beatles' quiet word
hookLine: a band with every stage open to it goes to an ashram on the Ganges
carry: japa: a sacred word repeated is an offering
tomorrow: say a word over and over and it goes empty. why not a mantra?
last: THE TRUE DEVOTEE FEELS ANOTHER'S PAIN.

cards: Some nights the only thing that quiets a loud head is one song on repeat. A well-known band, with every stage in the world open to it, went looking for something quieter than a song.
The Beatles traveled to an ashram in Rishikesh, a town on the Ganges at the foot of the Himalaya, to learn meditation from a teacher named Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. No crowds, no amplifiers.
And what he handed each of them wasn't anything you could hold. It was a word.

teach.b: The word is mantra. In English it can mean a slogan, something a coach repeats. On the Hindu path it's a sacred sound, word or verse, repeated with attention.

teach.h: JAPA, AND THE CLICK OF A MALA.
teach.b: The repeating has its own name, japa. Listen to how it sounds in a room: a murmur under the breath, the soft click of beads as a thumb moves one bead along for each round.

teach.h: A WORD THAT FITS IN A POCKET.
teach.b: That string of beads is a mala, and it lets the hand keep count so the mind doesn't have to. The Maharishi's students describe being given a mantra to repeat silently and easily, eyes closed. That made it portable.
A Beatle could carry it home to London. But the practice was old long before any band arrived.

teach.h: KRISHNA: AMONG OFFERINGS, I AM JAPA.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names places he can be found: among things that never move, the Himalaya; among rivers, the Ganges. And among offerings, he says, he is japa, the offering of repetition.
The quiet word, said again. Put the Beatles' story beside that list, and something lines up: the ashram on the Ganges, under the Himalaya, and a word repeated in silence.
In the Gita, all three are places Krishna can be found.

how: Hindus practice japa by repeating a mantra or a name of God, aloud, in a whisper or silently, often counting on a mala of beads at a home shrine or during the day.

games.q: what does “the beatles and the mantra” mean?
o: a pop song the band wrote after visiting India's holy places
a slogan the band used to stay motivated on long tours
a sacred word, repeated with attention, and a band that learned it

games.q: what's in the room — tap the pairs.
p: a sacred sound, word or verse

s: on the Hindu path, a mantra is just a motivating slogan
it's a sacred sound, word or verse, repeated with attention.
in the Gita, Krishna says that among offerings he is japa
the quiet repeated word sits in his list beside the Himalaya and the Ganges.

games.q: a friend's yoga teacher gives a 'mantra of the week': i am enough. is that a mantra in the Hindu sense?
o: not quite: a Hindu mantra is a sacred sound or word, repeated with attention.
yes: any phrase repeated often enough turns into a mantra.
no: a mantra only counts if it's in Sanskrit and said out loud.
games.why: on this path a mantra is sacred: a sound, word or verse repeated with attention, aloud or silently. a slogan is something else.

practice: Hold out one hand, palm up. Choose a word to say softly, a sacred word if you have one, or a plain one like peace, and say it once each time your thumb touches a fingertip, pointer to little finger and back again.
Let the thumb and the word keep the same slow pace, and feel the count happen in the hand.

wordCard.voice: The Beatles and the mantra: a band in Rishikesh, and an old practice, a sacred word repeated with attention.

orig.note: Sanskrit mantra: a sacred sound, word or verse, repeated in japa.

carryVoice: For the road, from the Beatles and the mantra: japa, a sacred word repeated, is an offering. More tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 10.25 (among offerings I am japa; among immovable things the Himalaya) and 10.31 (among rivers the Ganges)
